newsitem.title: THAILAND: Markets up despite Thai central bank chief's exit.
newsitem.headline: Markets up despite Thai central bank chief's exit.

text.p: Thai financial markets rallied on Tuesday despite news of the abrupt departure of central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond as exuberance over IMF involvement in reviving the battered economy overshadowed his resignation.

"I'm not saying that this is a good news. But the news that the government might turn to IMF facilities to turn the battered economy around lifted market gloom and whatever else seemed to matter less," said a currency dealer at a major U.S. bank.
The Thai baht rallied to 30.45 per dollar in the onshore market after hovering below 31.50 level since late last week.
The stock index roared up nearly two percent on the open. At 0319 GMT the index was up 9.27 points at 689.94.

"Investors weren't impressed with Rerngchai's performance during slightly over one year when he was in office. They thought he was a bit slow in solving problems, especially those related to financial institutions," said Thanawat Patchimkulk of Seamico Securities.

But analysts warned that the politics affecting the governor's job, especially as he presides over Thailand worst economic crisis in over a decade and gets ready to use bitter medicines to cure ills, would weigh on investor sentiment.
Rerngchai, who took office last July after his predecessor was forced out by political manoeuvring, submitted his resignation late on Monday and was not available for comment.
His resignation came as Thailand said it would accept the International Monetary Fund's advice and possibly loans to put the country back on track.
His term in office was marked by one of Thailand's biggest transitions as the country headed from boom to the worst bust in a decade.
Rerngchai was criticised after the authorities decided to put the baht into a managed float system after having pegged it to a trade-weighted basket of currencies for 13 years.
The government had hoped a managed float would induce foreign inflows to ease tight liquidity problems and bring down current high interest rates to resuscitate the ailing economy.

But analysts said lack of a solid and credible plan to support the baht after implementing the float caused the currency to lose about 20 percent of its value and fingers started pointing at the central bank chief.
Analysts said he would not be the only scapegoat.
"Whoever replaces (Rerngchai) will face the same pressure due to the negative economic outlook of the country," said Thamnu Wanglee, president of Nakornthon Bank.

Khanchit Assavasamran, economist at Vickers Ballas, said replacing central bank chiefs was not the answer to the Thailand's current woes and added that the overall government system needed to be overhauled.
"The perception of the public is the central bank moved very slow and tended to be conservative in handling the problems," he said.
"Sacking the governor is not the answer and not fair. What we need is a new working attitude, close cooperation, and concerted efforts in the same direction in solving the problems," he added.
